hints: Count the total electrons in a fluorine atom from its proton number, 9, then fill the orbitals in order of increasing energy starting with $1s$.
walkthrough:
Count electrons and fill in order**
Fluorine has atomic number 9, so a neutral atom has 9 electrons. Fill lowest energy first: $1s$ holds 2, $2s$ holds 2, leaving 5 to go into $2p$. That gives $1s^2 2s^2 2p^5$. Remember full configuration means writing every subshell out, not using shorthand.

hints: Write the configuration of oxygen in the n = 2 shell, $2s^2 2p^4$, then think how the four $2p$ electrons arrange singly before pairing.
walkthrough:
Picture the n = 2 electrons in oxygen**
Oxygen has 8 electrons total, with 6 in n = 2: $2s^2 2p^4$. The $2s$ subshell is full, so that is one pair. In $2p$, the four electrons occupy three orbitals as $\uparrow\downarrow$, $\uparrow$, $\uparrow$, giving one more paired set. So $1 + 1 = 2$ pairs in total.

hints: Work out the configuration of calcium, atomic number 20, and identify which subshell the last electrons enter, then recall the characteristic shape of that orbital type.
walkthrough:
Find the highest energy occupied orbital**
Calcium is element 20, configuration $1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^6 4s^2$. The $4s$ level is filled last and is highest in energy, even though n = 4 is a new shell. It is an s orbital.

Draw the s shape**
All s orbitals are spherical. A simple clear circle is enough, with no lobes or nodal planes. Do not draw a dumbbell, that is a p orbital and would lose the mark.

hints: Recall that first ionisation always starts from one mole of gaseous atoms and removes one electron to form a 1+ gaseous ion.
walkthrough:
Build the ionisation equation correctly**
First ionisation means removing the first electron from a gaseous atom. Start with $\text{S(g)}$. Remove one electron to give $\text{S}^{+}\text{(g)}$ plus $\text{e}^{-}$. Both sulfur species must be gas state symbols, and the equation must balance in charge as well as atoms.

hints: Compare the $3p$ arrangements of phosphorus, $3p^3$ with three unpaired electrons, and sulfur, $3p^4$ with one paired set.
Think about what extra repulsion exists when two electrons share the same $3p$ orbital, and how this compares with the small increase in nuclear charge from P to S.
walkthrough:
Compare the electron arrangements**
Phosphorus is $[\text{Ne}]3s^2 3p^3$, with one electron in each $3p$ orbital, all unpaired. Sulfur is $[\text{Ne}]3s^2 3p^4$, so one $3p$ orbital now contains a pair. The electron removed on first ionisation comes from that paired orbital.

Explain why pairing lowers the energy needed**
Two negative electrons sharing the same small orbital repel each other strongly. This spin pair repulsion pushes the electron to higher energy, so less energy is needed to remove it. Although sulfur has one more proton than phosphorus, which would normally raise ionisation energy, the repulsion effect is larger and dominates, so sulfur has the lower first ionisation energy.

Final answer: Sulfur has a pair of electrons in a $3p$ orbital whereas phosphorus has three unpaired $3p$ electrons.
The repulsion between the paired electrons in sulfur makes the electron easier to remove, and this outweighs the effect of the increased nuclear charge from P to S.

hints: Count the electrons in each species, $\text{F}^{-}$, $\text{Ne}$ and $\text{Na}^{+}$, to show they all have the same electronic arrangement.
List the proton numbers, F = 9, Ne = 10, Na = 11, and think which nucleus pulls most strongly on the same number of electrons.
Link greater proton number to greater pull on the outer electrons and therefore a smaller radius.
Use that logic to place the species with most protons as smallest and fewest protons as largest.
walkthrough:
Spot that they are isoelectronic**
Count electrons: $\text{F}^{-}$ is $9 + 1 = 10$, $\text{Ne}$ is 10, $\text{Na}^{+}$ is $11 - 1 = 10$. All have configuration $1s^2 2s^2 2p^6$. Same shells, same shielding, so size is decided only by nuclear charge.

Compare nuclear charge**
Proton numbers are $\text{F} = 9$, $\text{Ne} = 10$, $\text{Na} = 11$. With the same 10 electrons to attract, the $\text{Na}^{+}$ nucleus with 11 protons pulls hardest, $\text{F}^{-}$ with only 9 protons pulls weakest.

Link pull to radius**
Stronger nuclear attraction draws the same electron cloud in closer, shrinking the ion. Weaker attraction lets the cloud spread out. So radius decreases as proton number increases.

Write the order**
Smallest is the most pulled in, $\text{Na}^{+}$, then $\text{Ne}$, then largest is $\text{F}^{-}$: $\text{Na}^{+} < \text{Ne} < \text{F}^{-}$.

Final answer: $\text{Na}^{+} < \text{Ne} < \text{F}^{-}$ (smallest to largest).
All three species have the same number of electrons / are isoelectronic (10 electrons).
The larger the nuclear charge / number of protons, the stronger the attraction, so $\text{F}^{-}$ with fewest protons has the weakest nuclear attraction on its outer electrons and is largest.
